title: Key Counter With Instant Extremes
statement:
Build a counter of string keys that can always tell you a most-counted key and a least-counted key.

  • KeyTally() creates an empty counter.
  • inc(key) adds 1 to the count of key. A new key starts at count 1.
  • dec(key) subtracts 1 from the count of key. When a count reaches 0, the key is removed. dec is only called on keys that are present.
  • getMaxKey() returns a key with the highest count, or "" if the counter is empty.
  • getMinKey() returns a key with the lowest count, or "" if the counter is empty.

When several keys share the highest (or lowest) count, any one of them is accepted. Every operation must run in O(1) average time.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first one creates the counter. The output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned).

examples.why: "tab" reaches 2 and "menu" has 1. Two dec calls take "tab" back to 0, which removes it, so "menu" is now also the maximum.
An empty counter answers "". A key that drops to 0 is gone completely.

constraints: dec is only called on a key that is present
hints: A hash map from key to count makes inc and dec O(1). What is slow, and why can a heap not fix it cleanly?
Counts only ever change by 1. Group keys by their count, and keep the groups in a list sorted by count. Where does a key move after inc?

Use a doubly linked list of buckets, one per count that is in use, each holding a set of keys. A map points each key to its bucket. inc moves the key to the next bucket (creating it if its count is not exactly one more); dec moves it to the previous one. The first and last buckets give the min and max.

explain.intuition:
A map from key to count handles inc and dec, but finding the max or min would need a scan. A heap gives the max, but updating a key's count inside a heap is not O(1), and you need both ends at once.

The trick is that every change is by exactly 1. Put keys with the same count into one bucket, and chain the buckets in a doubly linked list sorted by count. When a key's count goes from c to c + 1 it moves from its bucket to the bucket right after it, or to a new bucket inserted right there. Nothing else in the list needs to shift. The list stays sorted on its own, so the first bucket always holds a min key and the last one a max key. A second map from key to its bucket finds the starting point in O(1). It is the same "map pointing into a linked list" design as an LRU cache.
steps: Keep sentinel buckets head (count 0) and tail (count ∞), and a map where from key to its bucket.

inc(key): let cur be its bucket, or head for a new key. If cur.next.count is not cur.count + 1, insert a new bucket after cur. Add the key there, update where, and remove it from cur (unless cur is head).
dec(key): if its count is 1, delete it from where. Otherwise move it to the bucket for count − 1 just before cur, creating that bucket if needed. Remove it from cur.
Whenever a bucket's key set becomes empty, unlink the bucket.
getMaxKey reads any key from tail.prev; getMinKey from head.next; return "" if the list is empty.
pitfalls: Unlinking the old bucket before inserting the new one next to it. The new bucket's position depends on the old one's neighbours.
Forgetting to delete empty buckets. Then getMinKey reads from a bucket with no keys.
Keeping a key with count 0 around after dec. It must disappear completely, or it would be reported as the minimum.

solutions.title: Count map with a scan for the extremes
solutions.idea: Keep only key → count. inc and dec are O(1); getMaxKey and getMinKey scan every key.
solutions.time: O(1) for inc/dec, O(k) for get

solutions.title: Linked list of count buckets
solutions.idea: Buckets of keys with the same count, in a doubly linked list sorted by count. A key moves at most one bucket per call, so every operation is O(1).

followups: Also support getting the count of any key and listing all keys with the current maximum count.
